title: Subordinate clauses: the one place ikke moves
goal: Join two sentences with *at*, *fordi*, *hvis* and *når* — then master the rule that reverses everything you've learned so far: inside a subordinate clause, *ikke* stands **in front of** the verb.
bekal: build subordinate clauses with seven conjunctions
move *ikke*, *alltid* and *aldri* in front of the verb inside a subordinate clause
invert the main clause when the subordinate clause comes first
wave: Review **unit 16** first: cover the Norwegian, look at the English, and rebuild the dialogue. Say ten strong verbs in all three forms.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Fordi jeg ikke forstår
dialogs.intro: An empty classroom after the lesson. Budi is still sitting at the back desk with an open book and a face that hides nothing.

lines.speaker: Læreren:
lines.text: Du ser ut som om du har et spørsmål.
lines.id: You look like you have a question.
lines.literal: you look out as if you have a question.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg tror at jeg har forstått alt — helt til jeg leser dette.
lines.id: I thought I'd understood everything — right up until I read this.
lines.literal: I believed that I had understood everything — completely until I read this.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: «Han sier at han ikke kommer.» Hvorfor står ikke etter han?
lines.id: "He said that he isn't coming." Why does *ikke* come after *han*?
lines.literal: "he said that he not comes." why stands not after he?

lines.speaker: Læreren:
lines.text: Fordi det er ei leddsetning. Der gjelder andre regler.
lines.id: Because it's a subordinate clause. Different rules apply there.
lines.literal: because it is a sub-clause. there apply other rules.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Så alt jeg har lært om ikke er feil?
lines.id: So everything I've learned about *ikke* is wrong?
lines.literal: so all I have learned about not is wrong?

lines.speaker: Læreren:
lines.text: Nei. Det gjelder fortsatt — bare ikke her. Hvis setningen begynner med at, fordi eller hvis, flytter ikke seg fram.
lines.id: No. It still applies — just not here. When the clause starts with *at*, *fordi* or *hvis*, *ikke* moves forward.
lines.literal: no. it applies still — only not here. when clause-the starts with that, because or if, moves not itself forward.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Og det er den eneste gangen?
lines.literal: and that is the only time-the?

lines.speaker: Læreren:
lines.text: Den eneste. Derfor er den lett å huske.
lines.id: The only one. That's why it's easy to remember.
lines.literal: the only. therefore is it easy to remember.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Når jeg ikke tenker på det, gjør jeg det riktig.
lines.id: When I don't think about it, I do it right.
lines.literal: when I not think on it, do I it right.

lines.speaker: Læreren:
lines.text: Da har du allerede lært det. Nå må du bare slutte å tenke.
lines.id: Then you've already learned it. Now you just have to stop thinking.
lines.literal: then have you already learned it. now must you only stop to think.

notes: **This is the only place in all of Norwegian where *ikke* stands in front of the verb** — and the order happens to match English exactly. *…at han **ikke kommer*** = "…that he **doesn't come**". After seventeen units of fighting your English habits, this unit gives one back.

**What is a subordinate clause?** A chunk that can't stand alone as a complete sentence and usually starts with *at*, *fordi*, *hvis*, *når*, *da*, *som* or *om*. If you cut it off and it feels left hanging, it's a subordinate clause.

**The V2 rule doesn't apply inside it.** In a main clause, the verb sits in second place; in a subordinate clause, the order is always **subject — (ikke) — verb**. No inversion, whatever comes before.

**Everything in slot four moves too**, not just *ikke*: *…at han **alltid** kommer*, *…fordi hun **aldri** spiser kjøtt*, *…hvis du **bare** hadde sagt det*. If you know the slot-four list from unit 7, you already know the list that moves here.

**Når jeg ikke tenker på det, gjør jeg det riktig** shows a second thing: when the subordinate clause comes **first**, the whole thing counts as slot one, so the main clause is **inverted**. Notice *gjør jeg*, not *jeg gjør*.
**Å se ut som om** means "to look as if". A fixed phrase; *som om* is a two-word conjunction that always stays together.

grammars.title: Seven conjunctions that open a subordinate clause
body: Learn these as one list. As soon as you see one of them, your hand should automatically put *ikke* in front of the verb.

head: Norsk
Say it
Meaning
Example
rows: *Jeg går fordi jeg ikke har tid.*
*Hvis du ikke vil, er det greit.*
*Da jeg ikke visste det, spurte jeg.*
*Boka som jeg ikke leste, var tykk.*
*Ring meg før du ikke rekker det.*
*Etter at vi hadde spist, gikk vi.*

after: ⚠️ **Når versus da** is the most common mistake newcomers make. *Da* is for a **single event in the past**; *når* is for **repeated** or **future** events. *Da jeg kom til Norge* (when I came, once) versus *når jeg kommer hjem* (whenever / when I get home).

⚠️ **Hvis versus om.** *Hvis* means "if" (condition); *om* means "whether" (indirect question). *Jeg vet ikke **om** han kommer* — I don't know **whether** he's coming. Using *hvis* there is wrong, even though English allows "if" in both.
*Som* covers everything English splits into *who*, *which* and *that*. One word for all three — a big saving.

grammars.title: Two word orders side by side
body: Read this table row by row and notice where *ikke* stands in each column.
after: The last row matters: when there's a helping verb, *ikke* goes in front of **the helping verb**, not the main verb. *…at han **ikke har sett** det*.
Quick test: cover the right column and convert every sentence in the left column yourself by putting *at* in front. If your hand doesn't move *ikke*, repeat this page tomorrow.

grammars.title: When the subordinate clause comes first
body: The whole subordinate clause counts as **one filler of slot one**. So the main clause is inverted — exactly the V2 rule from unit 3, nothing new.
after: A comma separates the two parts, and after the comma **the verb follows immediately**. If you write *Hvis du ikke vil, det er greit*, the sentence is wrong.
The reverse order needs no comma and inverts nothing: *Det er greit hvis du ikke vil.* Both are correct; putting it first stresses the condition.

sections.title: Verbs that need a reflexive pronoun

blocks.text: A number of Norwegian verbs always come with a pronoun pointing back to the subject — *meg*, *deg*, *seg*, *oss*, *dere*, *seg*. English handles most of them without any extra word, so this group has to be learned whole.

head: Norsk
Literally
English
rows: to go to bed, to lie down

blocks.text: The pronoun follows the subject: *jeg setter **meg***, *du setter **deg***, *han setter **seg***, *vi setter **oss***, *dere setter **dere***, *de setter **seg***. The form **seg** is used for every third person, singular and plural — one form covering four possibilities.
Inside a subordinate clause, this pronoun stays stuck to its verb and **doesn't move**: *…fordi jeg ikke føler meg bra*. Only *ikke* moves.
The ability to link sentences is what separates A1 from A2. These sentences are your tools.

head: Norsk
English
rows: *Jeg tror at det blir fint vær.*
I think the weather will be nice.
I don't know whether he's coming.
*Jeg går hjem fordi jeg er trøtt.*
I'm going home because I'm tired.
If it rains, we'll stay home.
*Når jeg kommer hjem, lager jeg mat.*
When I get home, I cook.
*Da jeg var barn, bodde jeg i Jakarta.*
When I was a child, I lived in Jakarta.
The man who lives there is a teacher.
I hope that you can come.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Take ten negative sentences from any unit, put *jeg tror at* in front, and move the *ikke*. Repeat until your hand does it on its own.
Then write five sentences starting with *hvis* or *når* and make sure the main clause is inverted after the comma.
Finally: tell the story of yesterday in five long sentences, each using one conjunction from the list. This is exactly the kind of answer the A2 oral exam will ask for.

exercises.prompt: Turn into a subordinate clause with *at*. Remember to move *ikke*.
items: Han kommer ikke. → Jeg tror at ____
Hun har ikke tid. → Jeg vet at ____
De spiser aldri kjøtt. → Han sier at ____
Det regner ofte her. → Alle vet at ____
Jeg forstår ikke alt. → Jeg innrømmer at ____
Han har ikke sett det. → Hun tror at ____
